opening.headline: When there is no criterion to determine whether a platform adequately supports AI workloads, we explore what common standards Kubernetes AI Conformance provides.
body: Imagine a scenario where three platform candidates all claim to support AI workloads. Yet, they differ significantly in how they request GPUs, support autoscaling, and provide accelerator metrics. Without a clear benchmark, any comparison simply becomes a comparison of marketing claims.

In this class, we examine what the CNCF's Kubernetes AI Conformance Program was designed to achieve and the procedures used for certification, including the difference between MUST and SHOULD requirements in the checklist, how to interpret status values, and how requirements vary across versions. Finally, we work through a case study comparing two candidate platforms based on conformance criteria.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the objectives and requirements of the AI Conformance Program
Suitability items can be differentiated based on platform selection criteria.

screens.title: Does this platform adequately support AI workloads?
screens.lead: When choosing a platform, take a moment to read common scenarios you'll encounter. Think about how you might distinguish between candidates who all say the same things.

visual.alt: Three platform candidates all promote the same phrase "AI supported," but their internal functionalities reveal distinctly different characteristics.
labels: What should we compare it to?

paragraphs: Platform candidates A, B, and C all claim to support AI workloads. However, upon closer examination, they differ significantly in how they handle GPU requests, whether auto-scaling functions properly, and the format in which metrics are presented.

AI workloads place unique pressure on clusters. This is because they often require accelerators, experience sudden traffic spikes, and demand strict isolation. As a result, applications that ran smoothly in one cluster may fail to run in another, giving rise to the well-known "it works in my cluster" issue.
Without clear criteria, platform comparisons merely become the side-by-side reading of statements each vendor promotes. What's needed is a common set of questions that can be asked of all candidates.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: What can actually be verified in the statement "Supports AI"? This course covers methods for transforming that statement into a verifiable claim.

screens.outro: First, let's directly consider the features that AI workloads require from a cluster.

screens.title: Functions that a cluster should have for AI workloads
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process unfolds. Please first mentally work through the answer before clicking it.

items.prompt: How do we request and distribute usage of accelerators like GPUs?
items.answer: Simply requesting acceleration via a simple count makes it difficult to express fine-grained requirements. We need approaches that allow more flexible device requests, as well as mechanisms where a single GPU is shared among multiple workloads.

items.prompt: How do we schedule training jobs that require multiple pods to be launched simultaneously?
items.answer: If some pods start while others remain in waiting state, no work is performed and resources are merely held. Group scheduling that ensures either all pods start or none do is required.

items.prompt: Does increased inference traffic lead to a proportional increase in pods and nodes? Are accelerator metrics available?
items.answer: Pod autoscaling and cluster autoscaling must also function when using a accelerator, and metrics such as accelerator utilization and memory must be exposed via standard mechanisms in order to enable operations. All of these questions are now candidates for compatibility items.

screens.outro: We will examine the structure of a program that groups questions under a common standard.

screens.title: Purpose and Structure of the AI Conformance Program
screens.lead: This examines the program step by step, starting with its purpose and the procedures used for authentication. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: A diagram showing AI readiness built upon basic Kubernetes readiness, illustrating the process from application to certification.

steps.title: Objective: Interoperability and common standards
steps.body: Kubernetes AI Conformance defines the capabilities that a Kubernetes platform must have to reliably run AI and machine learning workloads. The goal is to ensure that AI applications functioning on one compliant platform can operate seamlessly on other compliant platforms. It reduces the need for platform-specific workarounds and provides a foundational basis for the AI tooling ecosystem to build upon and validate.

steps.title: Target workloads
steps.body: We cover the most common AI/ML use cases: distributed or large-scale training requiring accelerators and predictable scheduling, model and LLM inference where latency, routing, and scalability are critical, and multi-step agent workloads that involve tools and memory in extended execution.

steps.title: Prerequisite: Basic suitability comes first
steps.body: The platform must first be Kubernetes conformant. AI compliance builds upon basic Kubernetes compliance, so AI certification can only be obtained without basic certification.

steps.title: Application: Checklist and public verification
steps.body: The core of the application materials is a public document link featuring a completed checklist and demonstrating how each requirement is satisfied. It resembles a structured self-assessment that can be reviewed. The application also includes the product logo and Kubernetes compatibility certification. The application process involves creating a Pull Request in a repository, which is then reviewed by the CNCF.

steps.title: Authentication unit and validity period
steps.body: Authentication is product-level and configuration-level. Even for the same product, cloud deployment and closed-network deployment represent different configurations and thus require separate authentication. Authentication is valid for one year and must be renewed with a new checklist before expiration.

screens.outro: I will now read one item from the checklist directly.

screens.title: Checklist item reading: MUST, SHOULD, status values
screens.lead: The following is an example based on a portion of a checklist. Select each highlighted section to verify the meanings of level and status.

data.text:
spec:
  schedulingOrchestration:
    - id: gang_scheduling
      level: MUST
      status: Implemented
      evidence:
        - "https://docs.example.com/platform/gang-scheduling"
      notes: ""
    - id: cluster_autoscaling
      level: MUST
      status: N/A
      notes: "Air-gapped configuration with a fixed node pool; no cluster autoscaler is shipped."
    - id: high_performance_networking
      level: SHOULD
      status: Partially Implemented
      evidence:
        - "https://docs.example.com/platform/multi-nic"
      notes: "Multiple network interfaces are supported; DRA-based management is not."

marks.note: MUST is a mandatory requirement that must be satisfied and must be verifiable. Here, gang_scheduling is designated as MUST and implemented, thus evidence is provided in the form of a public documentation link.
Evidence is a linked list of documents or test results that demonstrate fulfillment of requirements. If left blank, reviewers will be unable to verify compliance.

N/A does not mean that a feature is not supported. It means that the requirement does not apply in the given environment, and the rationale must be documented in the notes. The only conditional requirement in MUST items where N/A is accepted is cluster_autoscaling.

marks.span: notes: "Air-gapped configuration with a fixed node pool; no cluster autoscaler is shipped."
marks.note: The rationale for N/A should be "this requirement does not apply in this environment," rather than "this function is not supported." An example of such an environment is a closed-network configuration using a fixed node pool.

SHOULD indicates a recommendation. The status value must be one of Implemented, Not Implemented, Partially Implemented, or N/A. If partially implemented, noting the extent of implementation in the notes can be helpful for comparison.

screens.outro: Now let's examine how this checklist varies across different Kubernetes versions.

screens.title: Changes in requirements by version and ecosystem
screens.lead: Compare the checklists across Kubernetes versions in the table. The last row summarizes the ecosystem projects worth noting.

visual.alt: v1.35, v1.36, v1.37 checklist showing additions or omissions in the workflow.

data.caption: Version changes in the checklist
rows: In the acceleration area, `dra_support` must be present, while `driver_runtime_management`, `gpu_sharing`, and `virtualized_accelerator` should be present.
This was a mandatory requirement for DRA-based device requests.
In the checklist, the `dra_support` item is not visible, and `advanced_inference_ingress`, `high_performance_networking`, and `disaggregated_inference` should be added to the networking section.
Inference routing and standalone inference are recommended requirements.
`workload_sandboxing` should be added as SHOULD. Additionally, mixed verification enabling the combination of automated test results and manual proofs will become possible.
This addresses isolation requirements and changes to verification methods when an agent executes untrusted code.
This is a core requirement that demands proof in all three versions.
KServe is a multi-framework inference platform, and Kubeflow is a suite of tools that establishes an AI platform within Kubernetes. Both are CNCF projects.
Examples of AI tools commonly shared on suitable platforms.
data.notes: In version 1.37, requirements such as `secure_accelerator_access` and `gang_scheduling` include automated testing, while requirements without automated testing are proven through documented evidence. Items are added or removed across versions, so when evaluating a platform, one should base the checklist on the version of Kubernetes that matches their own.

screens.outro: Now we will compare the two candidate options under this item.

screens.title: Explanation: Example of comparing platform candidates against fit criteria
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the process of comparing candidates X and Y step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: A table-style diagram comparing candidates X and Y across suitability criteria.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: Assuming the cluster is operated based on Kubernetes v1.36, one of the platform candidates X or Y must be selected, both of which are introduced as well-supported for AI. Instead of relying on the promotional statements, a compatibility checklist is used uniformly for comparison.

steps.title: Step 1: Verify the premise
steps.body: First, verify whether the two candidates are fundamentally Kubernetes conformant, as AI compatibility builds upon this foundation. Then, confirm that the AI certification is applicable to the same Kubernetes version that we are using. Since checklists vary by version, certifications for different versions cannot be compared using the same language.

steps.title: Step 2: Compare the MUST row
steps.body: The MUST items in version 1.36 are `ai_inference`, `gang_scheduling`, `cluster_autoscaling`, `pod_autoscaling`, `accelerator_metrics`, `ai_service_metrics`, `secure_accelerator_access`, and `robust_controller`. Verify whether each item's status is implemented and whether the evidence link is publicly available and actually accessible. Evidence-free implementations are difficult to trust.

steps.title: Step 3: Review N/A
steps.body: Suppose candidate Y marked `cluster_autoscaling` as N/A for a closed-network configuration. This item is the only one among the MUST requirements that is conditionally specified, thus N/A may be accepted. However, it is necessary to distinguish whether the note states an environment description, such as "fixed node pool; does not provide cluster autoscaler," or a functional absence, such as "does not support." If our environment requires node expansion, then this N/A represents a substantive gap for us.

steps.title: Step 4: Should be tailored to our workloads.
steps.body: If MUST is similar, then SHOULD introduces the differences. If you plan to serve large models by splitting them into prefill and decode phases, `disaggregated_inference` is important; if fast inter-pod communication is critical, then `high_performance_networking` is important; if KV cache awareness or routing is required, then `advanced_inference_ingress` is important. We prioritize the items we need and evaluate the candidates accordingly.

steps.title: Step 5: Examine the composition and refresh timing
steps.body: Authentication applies to the product and its configuration and is valid for one year. We verify that the configuration we are using matches the certified configuration and that the certification is still within its valid period. Receiving cloud-based certification does not imply certification for a closed-network configuration.

steps.title: result
steps.body: The suitability criteria established a basis for presenting the two candidates side by side in the same language. This case's outcome enables us to identify specific items and evidence demonstrating differences between the candidates, without yet concluding which one is better.

screens.outro: I will summarize the decision-making approach derived from the case.

screens.title: Compatibility is a common language for platform selection
screens.lead: This lesson's content is summarized and organized from the perspective of platform selection.

paragraphs: AI Conformance is a CNCF program aimed at improving portability and establishing common standards for AI/ML workloads. Built upon basic Kubernetes compatibility, it targets training, inference, and agent-based workloads. Certification is issued at the product and configuration level and is valid for one year.

In a checklist, MUST items are essential requirements that must be satisfied along with evidence, while SHOULD items are recommendations. N/A does not mean "skip" but rather indicates that the requirement context does not apply to the environment. Requirements may be added or removed across versions, so it is necessary to review the checklist specific to your Kubernetes version.

When comparing platforms, these items become the common language: first verify the precondition, then contrast the proof of MUST, read the rationale for N/A, and finally align SHOULD with our workload.

Going back to the opening scene, even if all three candidates say they "support AI," we can now ask what specific items are satisfied by what kind of evidence. Comparing marketing claims becomes comparing verifiable criteria.

callout.label: organizing
callout.text: Compatibility is a common language for platform selection.

glossary.def: This is a CNCF program that defines platform capabilities required for AI/ML workloads and certifies them by product and configuration.
MUST is a mandatory requirement that must be satisfied with evidence, while SHOULD is a recommended requirement that may be omitted.
This is a state used when the context of the requirement does not apply to the environment, and the rationale must be explained in the notes.
This method, supported from version 1.37, involves submitting both automated test results and manual verification to apply for certification.
This is a CNCF project that comprises inference serving and AI platform tools within Kubernetes.

misconceptions.myth: If indicated as N/A, the requirement can be skipped.
misconceptions.fact: "Does not support" cannot be the basis for N/A. It must explain why the requirement does not apply in that environment, and conditional requirements are accepted only for the cluster_autoscaling feature.

misconceptions.myth: Having AI suitability certification is sufficient; basic Kubernetes authentication is not required.
misconceptions.fact: The platform must first be Kubernetes conformant. AI compatibility is built upon basic conformity.

misconceptions.myth: All checklist items for every Kubernetes version are the same.
misconceptions.fact: Items are added or removed across versions. For example, dra_support in version 1.35 does not appear in the version 1.36 checklist, but workload_sandboxing is added in version 1.37.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Compatibility is a common language for platform selection.
AI Conformance aims for portability and common standards and builds upon the basic Kubernetes certification.
MUST is mandatory and requires justification, SHOULD is recommended, and N/A requires justification for not applying to the environment.
Requirements vary by Kubernetes version, so refer to the appropriate checklist for your version.

checks.q: What is the correct interpretation when any item in the checklist is in an N/A state?
options: This means the feature is not supported, so the corresponding item is not satisfied.
Should be used only in SHOULD item; explanation is not required.
The MUST item has automatically been lowered to SHOULD.
Reasons for why the requirement does not apply to that environment must be documented in the notes.
checks.explain: N/A means the requirement does not apply in the given context, not the absence of support, and the rationale must be documented in the notes.

wrong.0: Not implemented indicates support is not available and should be distinguished from N/A.
wrong.1: Explanation is needed even for N/A.
wrong.2: N/A indicates whether the feature is applied, not a level change.

checks.intro: This question asks how to interpret the N/A status in a checklist. Recall the example you just read. The result is not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. N/A means the requirement does not apply, not that a function is missing.
checks.incorrectFeedback: If you interpreted N/A as not satisfied, that would be a misunderstanding. Please recall the difference between Not Implemented and N/A.

checks.q: Pair the terms and their meanings from a checklist.
right: Recommended guidelines that are not mandatory to fulfill
The context of the requirement is not applied to the environment, and the basis is noted in the notes.
Evidence and essential items that must be satisfied together
checks.explain: MUST must be satisfied with evidence, SHOULD is recommended, and N/A means not applicable, with the reason noted in the notes.
checks.intro: This is a question asking you to pair the meanings of MUST, SHOULD, and N/A. Results are not recorded, so please feel free to answer.
checks.correctFeedback: I accurately connected the meanings of these three terms.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is a mismatch. Please reclassify whether it is a mandatory requirement or a recommendation.

checks.q: When comparing platform candidates X and Y based on AI compatibility criteria, what is the first premise to verify?
options: Both are fundamentally Kubernetes conformant and use the same AI certification for the Kubernetes version.
How many additional features each candidate should support
Whether AI support is indicated in the candidate's marketing materials
Whether the two candidates are using the same cloud vendor's product
checks.explain: AI compatibility is built upon basic Kubernetes conformant foundations, and the checklists vary by version, so it's essential to first verify the version baseline before comparing in the same language.

wrong.1: Comparison SHOULD occur after verifying the MUST evidence and premises.
wrong.2: This program's starting point is that marketing copy cannot serve as a valid point of comparison.
wrong.3: Being the same is not a comparative premise.

checks.intro: This question asks you to select the premise to consider first when comparing candidates. Think about the structure in which authentication accumulates. The result is not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes, that's correct. Comparison must begin under the same criteria.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This is not a premise you need to verify before starting a comparison. Please recall once again on what foundation authentication is built.
